extracted.intended_audience: SNL viewers and general entertainment/TV comedy readers
extracted.subtask_short: editing sketch comedy for online release
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative guidance about how televised sketch comedy (specifically SNL) should be edited for online distribution, balancing polish with preservation of spontaneous, memorable moments. Discusses when dress-rehearsal or alternate footage helps or harms the comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of spontaneous moments
rubrics_metrics.description: It's the spontaneous moments that stand out; removing them takes away the spontaneous factor of comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: unscripted bits like 'Massive Head Wound Harry' (dog's off-script behavior) produce memorable laughs. Preserve on-air flubs or surprises that create unique comedic beats rather than replacing them with 'clean' footage. Anti-pattern: swapping in footage that erases or smooths over those surprises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performer commitment to the bit
rubrics_metrics.description: A great sketch will have a performer who completely commits to the bit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong performance commitment is a core ingredient of successful sketches; editing should not undercut or obscure that commitment. Evaluate clips for whether the performer’s choices and energy remain clear after edits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Premise richness
rubrics_metrics.description: A sketch should have a premise that's ripe with comedic material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even without spontaneous flubs, a strong, fertile premise can sustain a sketch. Editing can emphasize or blunt the premise — do not reshape a premise so it loses its comic potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve productive mistakes/imperfections
rubrics_metrics.description: If you remove the mistakes, you risk altering what could be a classic sketch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mistakes can create iconic moments (e.g., unexpected animal behavior). Avoid editing out errors that add humor or character. Use discretion: remove only when mistakes genuinely harm comprehension or pacing, not when they generate laughs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid manufactured-feeling online edits
rubrics_metrics.description: Online edits that feel manufactured take away the spontaneous factor of comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fans detect when footage is altered to look 'better' but loses authenticity. Anti-patterns include obviously spliced-in clips that change timing or reaction rhythms. Aim for edits that preserve the feel of a live performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage behind-the-scenes moments honestly
rubrics_metrics.description: Producers can lean into behind-the-scenes moments (dress rehearsals, goofs) when those moments are funnier or add charm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use behind-the-scenes footage as a feature when it enhances humor (e.g., the 'Debbie Downer' dress rehearsal airing with a disclaimer). If using rehearsal footage, be transparent or make clear the switch so context isn't misleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency about footage source
rubrics_metrics.description: Online videos should not present materially different or rehearsal-derived footage as the aired sketch without indication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fans noticed when online videos differed from what aired; labeling or disclaimers help maintain trust. Disclosing that a clip is from dress rehearsal avoids feelings of manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not alter core beats or character interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Edits should avoid changing fundamental narrative or interactional beats that define a scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: Star Wars 'special edition' changes that altered key moments (e.g., 'Han Shot First') were received poorly. Similarly, changing who reacts or how a beat lands can change a sketch's meaning or humor. Preserve original intent and timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid jarring, unnecessary enhancements
rubrics_metrics.description: Some changes or enhancements may be jarring and stick out, undermining the scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from film: intrusive CGI or ill-fitting additions. For sketch comedy, avoid overlays, insertions, or corrections that clash with the show's established tone and production values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect the show's creative spark and cast chemistry
rubrics_metrics.description: Editing choices should not accelerate loss of the cast's creative spark or hollow out sketches that rely on chemistry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seasonal cast departures already risk diminishing creativity; heavy-handed editing that sanitizes or homogenizes performances can further alienate audiences. Prioritize preserving the energy and risk-taking that drive memorable moments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resist technological temptation to over-polish
rubrics_metrics.description: Having the technology to replace or 'fix' moments doesn't mean it should be used; over-polishing can erase what made moments special.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Question whether a tech-enabled fix improves or diminishes the humor. When the raw take carries comedic value, prefer authenticity over a technically 'perfect' but less funny version.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use edits to enhance, not rewrite, the historical record
rubrics_metrics.description: Editing archival or classic material should respect its original cultural standing and audience memory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fans often value original versions (requests to show original Star Wars cuts); altering historical comedy moments risks audience backlash. If edits are necessary, consider preserving originals or presenting both versions.
